claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels cluster in macromolecular complexes at nodes of Ranvier to promote rapid nerve impulse conduction in vertebrate nerves.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels cluster in macromolecular complexes at nodes of Ranvier to promote rapid nerve impulse conduction in vertebrate nerves.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Node assembly in peripheral nerves is thought to be initiated at heminodes at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Node assembly in peripheral nerves is thought to be initiated at heminodes at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells, and fusion of heminodes results in the establishment of nodes.
evidence: This represents the prevailing model in the field prior to this study, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Fusion of heminodes results in the establishment of nodes.
source: Node assembly in peripheral nerves is thought to be initiated at heminodes at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells, and fusion of heminodes results in the establishment of nodes.
evidence: This is part of the established model of node formation in peripheral nerves.

claim: Assembly of 'early clusters' of nodal proteins in the murine axonal membrane precedes heminode formation.
source: Here we show that assembly of 'early clusters' of nodal proteins in the murine axonal membrane precedes heminode formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by temporal quantification data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The neurofascin (Nfasc) proteins are essential for node assembly.
source: The neurofascin (Nfasc) proteins are essential for node assembly, and the formation of early clusters also requires neuronal Nfasc.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the introduction and confirmed by the authors' experiments with Nfasc-null neurons.

claim: The formation of early clusters requires neuronal Nfasc.
source: The neurofascin (Nfasc) proteins are essential for node assembly, and the formation of early clusters also requires neuronal Nfasc.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that early clusters are barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons compared to Nfasc+/+ neurons.

claim: Early clusters are mobile.
source: Early clusters are mobile and their proteins are dynamically recruited by lateral diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing early clusters moving along axons (Figure 5, Videos 3-5).

claim: Proteins in early clusters are dynamically recruited by lateral diffusion.
source: Early clusters are mobile and their proteins are dynamically recruited by lateral diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP and FRAP/FLIP experiments showing that fluorescence recovery at early clusters is prevented when lateral diffusion is blocked (Figure 3).

claim: Early clusters can undergo fusion with each other.
source: They can undergo fusion not only with each other but also with heminodes, thus contributing to the development of nodes in peripheral axons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing multiple early clusters merging (Figure 7A, Video 6).

claim: Early clusters can undergo fusion with heminodes.
source: They can undergo fusion not only with each other but also with heminodes, thus contributing to the development of nodes in peripheral axons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing an early cluster merging with a heminode (Figure 7B, Video 7).

claim: Early clusters contribute to the development of nodes in peripheral axons.
source: They can undergo fusion not only with each other but also with heminodes, thus contributing to the development of nodes in peripheral axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early clusters can fuse with heminodes, which are precursors to nodes, and from the temporal relationship showing early clusters appear first and decline as heminodes and nodes increase.

claim: The formation of early clusters constitutes the earliest stage in peripheral node assembly.
source: The formation of early clusters constitutes the earliest stage in peripheral node assembly and expands the repertoire of strategies that have evolved to establish these essential structures.
evidence: This is supported by temporal data showing early clusters appear before heminodes and nodes both in vitro and in vivo (Figure 6).

claim: The Nfasc gene is essential for node formation.
source: Much has been learned about the composition and assembly of nodes, such as the role of proteins encoded by the neurofascin (Nfasc) gene, which is essential for node formation; nevertheless, how myelinating Schwann cells initiate the assembly of macromolecular axonal complexes containing Nav is still incompletely understood (Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020; Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020; Rasband and Peles, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research and confirmed by the authors' experiments.

claim: Nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin on naked peripheral axonal segments have been observed in myelinating co-cultures of Schwann cells with neurons from dorsal root ganglia (DRG).
source: Although heminodes are thought to initiate node formation (Rasband and Peles, 2021), nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin on naked peripheral axonal segments have been observed in myelinating co-cultures of Schwann cells with neurons from dorsal root ganglia (DRG) (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), in developing wild-type (WT) mouse sciatic nerves (Lambert et al., 1997) and in the peripheral nerves of control mice with floxed alleles that were phenotypically normal (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020; Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin have been observed in developing wild-type (WT) mouse sciatic nerves.
source: Although heminodes are thought to initiate node formation (Rasband and Peles, 2021), nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin on naked peripheral axonal segments have been observed in myelinating co-cultures of Schwann cells with neurons from dorsal root ganglia (DRG) (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), in developing wild-type (WT) mouse sciatic nerves (Lambert et al., 1997) and in the peripheral nerves of control mice with floxed alleles that were phenotypically normal (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020; Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambert et al., 1997.

claim: Nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin have been observed in the peripheral nerves of control mice with floxed alleles that were phenotypically normal.
source: Although heminodes are thought to initiate node formation (Rasband and Peles, 2021), nodal protein complexes lacking either flanking Schwann cells or myelin on naked peripheral axonal segments have been observed in myelinating co-cultures of Schwann cells with neurons from dorsal root ganglia (DRG) (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), in developing wild-type (WT) mouse sciatic nerves (Lambert et al., 1997) and in the peripheral nerves of control mice with floxed alleles that were phenotypically normal (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020; Muir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020 and Muir et al., 2014.

claim: Myelinating axons with 'node-like clusters' display an enhanced conduction velocity in vivo.
source: In vivo, myelinating axons with these 'node-like clusters' display an enhanced conduction velocity (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), and similar structures accelerate conduction speeds in premyelinated axons of the central nervous system (CNS) (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Similar structures to 'node-like clusters' accelerate conduction speeds in premyelinated axons of the central nervous system (CNS).
source: In vivo, myelinating axons with these 'node-like clusters' display an enhanced conduction velocity (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), and similar structures accelerate conduction speeds in premyelinated axons of the central nervous system (CNS) (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2015.

claim: Early clusters are the earliest detectable Nav-rich complexes of nodal proteins in primary sensory neurons.
source: Here we show that 'node-like clusters' are the earliest detectable Nav-rich complexes of nodal proteins in primary sensory neurons, and their appearance requires the presence of myelinating Schwann cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal quantification showing early clusters appear before heminodes and nodes (Figure 6).

claim: The appearance of early clusters requires the presence of myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Here we show that 'node-like clusters' are the earliest detectable Nav-rich complexes of nodal proteins in primary sensory neurons, and their appearance requires the presence of myelinating Schwann cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that early clusters do not form in the absence of Schwann cells or when Schwann cells are not induced to myelinate (Figure 2A).

claim: The emergence of early clusters anticipates that of heminodes.
source: Since their emergence anticipates that of heminodes, we describe them as early clusters.
evidence: This is supported by temporal data showing early clusters appear before heminodes (Figure 6).

claim: Unlike heminodes, which are associated with Schwann cell microvilli, nucleation of early clusters is not spatially restricted to sites of any apparent axo-glial structural specialisation.
source: Unlike heminodes, which are associated with Schwann cell microvilli, nucleation of early clusters is not spatially restricted to sites of any apparent axo-glial structural specialisation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining showing absence of microvillar markers at early clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and by CLEM showing no ultrastructural specializations (Figure 2C).

claim: Nodal proteins are recruited to early clusters by lateral diffusion in the plane of the axonal membrane and not by direct fusion of vesicular transport vesicles.
source: Furthermore, nodal proteins are recruited to early clusters by lateral diffusion in the plane of the axonal membrane and not by direct fusion of vesicular transport vesicles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments showing that fluorescence recovery is completely prevented when lateral diffusion is blocked (Figure 3D, E, G).

claim: Nucleation of early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture requires neuronal neurofascin 186 (Nfasc186).
source: Nucleation of early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture requires neuronal neurofascin 186 (Nfasc186) but is independent of the establishment of axo-glial junctions mediated by the interaction of Caspr with glial neurofascin 155.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing early clusters are barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons.

claim: Nucleation of early clusters is independent of the establishment of axo-glial junctions mediated by the interaction of Caspr with glial neurofascin 155.
source: Nucleation of early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture requires neuronal neurofascin 186 (Nfasc186) but is independent of the establishment of axo-glial junctions mediated by the interaction of Caspr with glial neurofascin 155.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that early cluster assembly is unaffected in Caspr-null neurons (Figure 4).

claim: Either the glial or the neuronal isoforms of the Nfasc gene are required for Nav recruitment to PNS nodes of Ranvier.
source: This is consistent with the requirement of either the glial or the neuronal isoforms of the Nfasc gene for Nav recruitment to PNS nodes of Ranvier (Amor et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015) but contrasts with the fact that neurofascins are neither required for the formation of early clusters in the CNS, nor is neuronal Nfasc an obligate component of these early clusters (pre-nodes) (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Amor et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Neurofascins are not required for the formation of early clusters in the CNS.
source: This is consistent with the requirement of either the glial or the neuronal isoforms of the Nfasc gene for Nav recruitment to PNS nodes of Ranvier (Amor et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015) but contrasts with the fact that neurofascins are neither required for the formation of early clusters in the CNS, nor is neuronal Nfasc an obligate component of these early clusters (pre-nodes) (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2015.

claim: Neuronal Nfasc is not an obligate component of early clusters (pre-nodes) in the CNS.
source: This is consistent with the requirement of either the glial or the neuronal isoforms of the Nfasc gene for Nav recruitment to PNS nodes of Ranvier (Amor et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015) but contrasts with the fact that neurofascins are neither required for the formation of early clusters in the CNS, nor is neuronal Nfasc an obligate component of these early clusters (pre-nodes) (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2015.

claim: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are highly dynamic.
source: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are mobile and highly dynamic and can disintegrate or fuse with each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery (Figure 3) and time-lapse imaging showing movement and fusion (Figure 5, Figure 7).

claim: Early clusters can disintegrate.
source: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are mobile and highly dynamic and can disintegrate or fuse with each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing an early cluster fragmenting and disappearing (Figure 5C, Video 4).

claim: Mobile early clusters can fuse with neighbouring heminodes.
source: This view is supported by the ability of these mobile early clusters to fuse with neighbouring heminodes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing an early cluster merging with a heminode (Figure 7B, Video 7).

claim: Dynamic early clusters of nodal proteins in PNS nerves represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly during myelination that precedes heminode formation.
source: We show that dynamic early clusters of nodal proteins in PNS nerves represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly during myelination that precedes heminode formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including temporal analysis, Nfasc dependency, and fusion with heminodes.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are targeted to the axonal plasma membrane during myelination by Schwann cells.
source: First, we showed that SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are targeted appropriately to the axonal membrane during myelination (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging and immunostaining shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Before myelin ensheathment, both SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP were diffusely distributed along the axolemma.
source: Before myelin ensheathment, both proteins were diffusely distributed along the axolemma but became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment.
source: Before myelin ensheathment, both proteins were diffusely distributed along the axolemma but became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Early clusters containing fluorescently tagged Nfasc186 or β1Nav are nodal protein complexes.
source: Early clusters containing fluorescently tagged Nfasc186 or β1Nav are nodal protein complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining showing colocalization with nodal markers AnkG and βIV-spectrin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: The transgenic fusion proteins SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are appropriate surrogate markers for detecting early clusters, heminodes, and nodes by live imaging.
source: Hence, the transgenic fusion proteins are appropriate surrogate markers for detecting early clusters, heminodes, and nodes by live imaging.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins localize correctly to nodal structures and colocalize with endogenous nodal markers.

claim: β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters were barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons compared to Nfasc+/+ neurons.
source: Although β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters assembled in Nfasc+/+ neurons, they were barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons (β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters/100 neurons, mean ± SEM: Nfasc+/+, 25.40 ± 5.60; Nfasc-/-, 0.21 ± 0.05; p = 0.0107, two-tailed unpaired student's t-test, n = 3 independent cultures).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison showing statistically significant difference (p = 0.0107).

claim: Glial neurofascin isoform Nfasc155 plays no part in early cluster formation.
source: These co-cultures are not completely neurofascin-null since WT Schwann cells express the glial neurofascin isoform, Nfasc155. However, this isoform clearly plays no part in early cluster formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early clusters do not form in Nfasc-/- neurons even though WT Schwann cells expressing Nfasc155 are present.

claim: Neuronal neurofascin is necessary for the assembly of early clusters.
source: Hence, neuronal neurofascin is not only important in node formation but also necessary for the assembly of early clusters.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the absence of early clusters in Nfasc-/- neurons.

claim: Schwann cells are required for early cluster formation.
source: Therefore, we wished to explore the dependency of early cluster formation on Schwann cells. We showed that not only were Schwann cells required for early cluster formation but also they must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing early clusters do not form without Schwann cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Schwann cells must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid for early cluster formation.
source: Therefore, we wished to explore the dependency of early cluster formation on Schwann cells. We showed that not only were Schwann cells required for early cluster formation but also they must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments comparing conditions with and without myelinating medium (Figure 2A).

claim: Laminin stimulates myelination and enhanced early cluster formation.
source: Laminin, a component of matrigel, stimulates myelination and enhanced early cluster formation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing early cluster formation in matrigel-coated versus collagen-coated chambers (Figure 2A).

claim: The presence of Schwann cells alone is not sufficient for early cluster formation.
source: Hence, the presence of Schwann cells alone is not sufficient for early cluster formation, but they must also be myelinating.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing early clusters do not form when Schwann cells are present but not induced to myelinate (Figure 2A).

claim: Schwann cell microvillar markers including pERM, dystrophin isoform 116 (Dp116), and radixin are not detectable at early clusters.
source: However, although gliomedin is also found in the microvilli at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells (Eshed et al., 2005), no other Schwann cell microvillar markers, including pERM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), dystrophin isoform 116 (Dp116), and radixin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), were detectable at early clusters, despite being strongly enriched at heminodes and nodes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli.
source: Thus, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of microvillar markers at early clusters.

claim: CLEM confirmed the close contact between Schwann cells and axons at early clusters.
source: CLEM confirmed the close contact between Schwann cells and axons at early clusters (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlative light and electron microscopy shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CLEM did not reveal any axo-glial ultrastructural specialisations at early clusters that might contribute to their formation.
source: These results underscored the close physical proximity of Schwann cells and axonal early clusters but did not reveal any axo-glial ultrastructural specialisations that might contribute to their formation.
evidence: This is based on examination of serial EM sections shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mature nodes are very stable structures.
source: Mature nodes are very stable structures (Zonta et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zonta et al., 2011 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool.
source: In contrast, heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool (Zhang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2020, and confirmed by the authors' FRAP experiments.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 expressed on the axons of neurons cultured without Schwann cells was highly mobile.
source: SEP-Nfasc186 expressed on the axons of neurons cultured without Schwann cells was highly mobile (Figure 3A–C; Video 1), which was consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2012; Ghosh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C and Video 1.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile than on unmyelinated axons, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures.
source: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures, whereas nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile.
source: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures, whereas nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing minimal fluorescence recovery at nodes (Figure 3A-C).

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes displayed mobilities intermediate between early clusters and nodes.
source: SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes displayed mobilities intermediate between early clusters and nodes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal clusters gradually declines as it acquires more mature features.
source: Thus, the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal clusters gradually declines as it acquires more mature features.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mobility decreases from unmyelinated axons to early clusters to heminodes to nodes.

claim: Heminodes are dynamic structures that can rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool.
source: Our observation that heminodes are dynamic structures is particularly intriguing and represents the first direct demonstration that, unlike nodes, they can rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery at heminodes (Figure 3).

claim: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters.
source: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters (Figure 3D,E and G; Video 2), indicating that SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at these structures is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3D, E, G and Video 2.

claim: SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at early clusters is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
source: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters (Figure 3D,E and G; Video 2), indicating that SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at these structures is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments showing no recovery when lateral diffusion is blocked (Figure 3D, E, G).

claim: Fluorescence recovery at heminodes is predominantly mediated by the pool of SEP-Nfasc186 on the flanking unmyelinated axon.
source: Interestingly, FRAP/FLIP showed that the same mode of fluorescence recovery applies to heminodes and that this recovery is predominantly mediated by the pool of SEP-Nfasc186 on the flanking unmyelinated axon (Figure 3D,F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by asymmetric FLIP experiments showing recovery is prevented when the unmyelinated side is photobleached (Figure 3D, F, G).

claim: Neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP.
source: We found that neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of this membrane protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of vesicle movement before and after FLIP shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of β1Nav-EGFP.
source: We found that neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of this membrane protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vesicle movement is unchanged after FLIP.

claim: β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile.
source: Thus, like SEP-Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile, but its turnover rate is considerably slower.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery at β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).

claim: The turnover rate of β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is considerably slower than SEP-Nfasc186.
source: Thus, like SEP-Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile, but its turnover rate is considerably slower.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that β1Nav-EGFP requires 4 hours to recover to levels comparable to SEP-Nfasc186.

claim: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons.
source: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D) but had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of vesicle movement shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: Nocodazole treatment had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching.
source: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D) but had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments in the presence of nocodazole shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F.

claim: β1Nav-EGFP fluorescence in early clusters recovers by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane.
source: This indicated that, like Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP fluorescence in early clusters recovers by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nocodazole, which blocks vesicular transport, does not affect fluorescence recovery at early clusters.

claim: Fluorescence recovery of SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters is unaffected in Caspr-null DRG axons from Cntnap1-/- mice.
source: Since distinct axo-glial specialisations are not apparent at the ultrastructural level in their vicinity (Figure 2C), we predicted that fluorescence recovery of SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters would be unaffected in Caspr-null DRG axons from Cntnap1-/- mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing similar recovery in Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- early clusters (Figure 4A, B, C).

claim: The absence of Caspr did not influence the assembly of early clusters.
source: Furthermore, the absence of Caspr, and hence of paranodal axo-glial junctions (Bhat et al., 2001), did not influence the assembly of early clusters (SEP-Nfasc186+ early clusters/100 neurons; mean ± SEM: Cntnap1+/+, 90.2 ± 28.3; Cntnap1-/-, 90.9 ± 15.0; p = 0.9838; two-tailed paired student's t-test; n = 3 independent cultures).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification showing no significant difference in early cluster numbers between Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- (p = 0.9838).

claim: Loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes, but, and consistent with earlier reports (Zhang et al., 2020), junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4A, B, C.

claim: Junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes, but, and consistent with earlier reports (Zhang et al., 2020), junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing increased recovery at Cntnap1-/- nodes compared to WT nodes (Figure 4A, B, C).

claim: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption reflects the dominant contribution of fluorescence recovery of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction.
source: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption presumably reflects the dominant contribution of fluorescence recovery of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction (Figure 3D,F and G).
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric FLIP experiments showing recovery is predominantly from the unmyelinated side.

claim: The ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP.
source: We observed that the ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes.
source: Furthermore, while FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes, it resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: FLIP resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes.
source: Furthermore, while FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes, it resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Paranodal axo-glial junctions act as diffusion barriers that stabilize nodes.
source: Using FRAP and FRAP/FLIP, we now provide direct evidence for this. We observed that the ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that in the absence of paranodal junctions, nodes can exchange proteins with the axonal pool, and this exchange is blocked by FLIP.

claim: The formation of axo-glial junctions has a profound effect on the dynamic properties of mature nodal assemblies.
source: Collectively, these results support the view that early clusters are highly dynamic structures untrammelled by axo-glial interactions and further demonstrate that the formation of axo-glial junctions has a profound effect on the dynamic properties of mature nodal assemblies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nodes without paranodal junctions are more dynamic than WT nodes.

claim: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period.
source: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period and appeared to migrate along the axon (Figure 5A; Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Video 3.

claim: Early clusters appeared to migrate along the axon.
source: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period and appeared to migrate along the axon (Figure 5A; Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Video 3.

claim: The perceived movement of early clusters could not be explained by axonal extension.
source: When the position of early clusters was recorded in relation to immobile landmarks, such as axonal branching points or points of intersection with other axons, it became apparent that the perceived movement of early clusters could not be explained by axonal extension (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking early clusters relative to fixed landmarks shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When multiple early clusters were present on the same axonal segment, they almost invariably moved synchronously in the same direction and at the same speed.
source: Interestingly, when multiple early clusters were present on the same axonal segment, they almost invariably moved synchronously in the same direction and at the same speed (Figure 5D; Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5D and Video 5.

claim: Treatment with latrunculin A strongly impaired the movement of early clusters.
source: Treatment with latrunculin A strongly impaired the movement of early clusters, significantly reducing both the percentage and the speed of early clusters that were mobile (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement in the presence of latrunculin A shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Latrunculin A effectively disrupted the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Latrunculin A effectively disrupted the actin cytoskeleton, as evidenced by the dramatic reduction in the intensity of phalloidin staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters.
source: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters, indicating that myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons (mean ± SEM: dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 0.99 ± 0.09 μm/s; blebbistatin, 0.70 ± 0.03, p = 0.0233, two-tailed paired student's t-test, n = 4 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification showing statistically significant reduction in speed (p = 0.0233).

claim: Myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons.
source: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters, indicating that myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons (mean ± SEM: dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 0.99 ± 0.09 μm/s; blebbistatin, 0.70 ± 0.03, p = 0.0233, two-tailed paired student's t-test, n = 4 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blebbistatin, a myosin II inhibitor, reduces early cluster speed.

claim: Node-like clusters were consistently observed 5 days after the induction of myelination, a stage at which no heminodes or nodes were detectable.
source: We consistently observed node-like clusters 5 days after the induction of myelination, a stage at which no heminodes or nodes were detectable (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes.
source: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification over time shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The number of early clusters steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination.
source: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification over time shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment.
source: Although the appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment (Figure 6A), we also found, consistent with what we had observed in the somal compartment, that the initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in both compartments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment.
source: Although the appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment (Figure 6A), we also found, consistent with what we had observed in the somal compartment, that the initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in the axonal compartment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Assembly of early clusters proceeds sequentially in a somal-to-distal direction in vitro.
source: This indicates that, like heminodes and nodes, assembly of early clusters proceeds sequentially in a somal-to-distal direction in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early clusters appear earlier in the somal compartment than in the distal axonal compartment.

claim: The sequential appearance of early clusters, followed by heminodes, followed by nodes, observed in co-cultures, was also observed in vivo.
source: The sequential appearance of early clusters, followed by heminodes, followed by nodes, observed in co-cultures, was also observed in vivo (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in sciatic nerves at P1, P3, and P5 shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Early cluster assembly is a temporally regulated developmental stage of PNS myelination both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Taken together, our data show that early cluster assembly is a temporally regulated developmental stage of PNS myelination both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis showing early clusters appear first, peak, and then decline as heminodes and nodes increase, both in culture and in vivo.

claim: The vast majority of early clusters were mobile (84.2 ± 2.2%).
source: We found that the vast majority of early clusters were mobile (% of mobile early clusters, mean ± SEM, 84.2 ± 2.2, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture) and progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h (mean ± SEM, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement.

claim: Early clusters progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h.
source: We found that the vast majority of early clusters were mobile (% of mobile early clusters, mean ± SEM, 84.2 ± 2.2, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture) and progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h (mean ± SEM, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement speed.

claim: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode.
source: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode, while no early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of early cluster movement direction relative to heminodes.

claim: No early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
source: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode, while no early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of early cluster movement direction.

claim: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment.
source: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Early clusters can migrate towards and contribute to heminode formation.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that early clusters can migrate towards and contribute to heminode formation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing early clusters fusing with heminodes (Figure 7B) and the model in Figure 7C.

claim: Early clusters are the earliest nodal complexes in the pathway to the assembly of the node of Ranvier in culture and in vivo.
source: Hence, they are the earliest nodal complexes in the pathway to the assembly of the node of Ranvier in culture and in vivo (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis and fusion observations, and supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models.
source: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models and severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans (Sherman et al., 2005; Maluenda et al., 2016; Wambach et al., 2017; Laquérriere et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2017; Mehta et al., 2017; Conant et al., 2018; Nizon et al., 2017; Monfrini et al., 2019; Smigiel et al., 2018; SYNAPS Study Group et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Disruption of nodal complex assembly results in severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans.
source: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models and severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans (Sherman et al., 2005; Maluenda et al., 2016; Wambach et al., 2017; Laquérriere et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2017; Mehta et al., 2017; Conant et al., 2018; Nizon et al., 2017; Monfrini et al., 2019; Smigiel et al., 2018; SYNAPS Study Group et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: When expressed in Nfasc-null mice, the neuronal isoform Nfasc186 has the ability to cluster Nav at PNS nodes in the absence of the glial isoform, Nfasc155.
source: When expressed in Nfasc-null mice in which nodal complexes cannot assemble, the neuronal isoform Nfasc186 has the ability to cluster Nav at PNS nodes in the absence of the glial isoform, Nfasc155 (Sherman et al., 2005; Zonta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sherman et al., 2005 and Zonta et al., 2008.

claim: When glial Nfasc155 and its paranodal adhesion complex with contactin and Caspr are intact, nodes assemble in the absence of neuronal Nfasc186.
source: Furthermore, the converse is true: when glial Nfasc155 and its paranodal adhesion complex with contactin and Caspr are intact, nodes assemble in the absence of neuronal Nfasc186 (Amor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amor et al., 2017.

claim: Heminodal clustering of nodal complexes is widely considered to be the initial step in PNS nodal assembly.
source: Heminodal clustering of nodal complexes is widely considered to be the initial step in PNS nodal assembly (Rasband and Peles, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rasband and Peles, 2021.

claim: Heminodal complexes form at the tips of the microvillar structures located at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Heminodal complexes form at the tips of the microvillar structures located at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells (Ching et al., 1999; Schafer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ching et al., 1999 and Schafer et al., 2006.

claim: Accumulation of the Schwann cell microvillar protein gliomedin drives the focal recruitment of neuronal Nfasc186, and in turn, AnkG, βIV-spectrin, and Nav at heminodes.
source: Accumulation of the Schwann cell microvillar protein gliomedin drives the focal recruitment of neuronal Nfasc186, and in turn, AnkG, βIV-spectrin, and Nav at heminodes (Eshed et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed et al., 2005.

claim: Convergence and fusion of heminodal complexes gives rise to mature nodes.
source: Subsequent convergence and fusion of these heminodal complexes gives rise to mature nodes.
evidence: This represents the established model of node formation.

claim: Axo-glial junctions are proposed to act as advancing diffusion barriers that restrict the localisation of axolemma-expressed Nav to the gaps between growing myelin segments.
source: Axo-glial junctions are proposed to act as advancing diffusion barriers that restrict the localisation of axolemma-expressed Nav to the gaps between growing myelin segments (Rasband and Peles, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rasband and Peles, 2016.

claim: As adjacent paranodal axo-glial junctions converge, they gradually concentrate Nav in the diminishing gap between them, ultimately resulting in their focal accumulation at nodes.
source: As adjacent paranodal axo-glial junctions converge, they are believed to gradually concentrate Nav in the diminishing gap between them, ultimately resulting in their focal accumulation at nodes (Rasband and Peles, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rasband and Peles, 2016.

claim: Genetic ablation of gliomedin suppresses heminode formation.
source: Genetic ablation of gliomedin suppresses heminode formation (Feinberg et al., 2010), while deletion of either Caspr, Nfasc155, or contactin prevents the establishment of paranodal axo-glial junctions (Pillai et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2001; Boyle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Feinberg et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of either Caspr, Nfasc155, or contactin prevents the establishment of paranodal axo-glial junctions.
source: Genetic ablation of gliomedin suppresses heminode formation (Feinberg et al., 2010), while deletion of either Caspr, Nfasc155, or contactin prevents the establishment of paranodal axo-glial junctions (Pillai et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2001; Boyle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pillai et al., 2009; Bhat et al., 2001; Boyle et al., 2001.

claim: Neither loss of gliomedin nor disruption of paranodal junctions is sufficient to prevent peripheral node formation.
source: Nevertheless, neither insult is sufficient to prevent peripheral node formation: when one mechanism fails, the other can rescue node assembly.
evidence: This represents the concept of redundancy in node assembly mechanisms.

claim: In the CNS, both paranodal axo-glial junctions and specialised interactions between nodal extracellular matrix proteins and Nfasc186 support node formation.
source: Mechanisms of node assembly are similarly redundant in the CNS. There, both paranodal axo-glial junctions and specialised interactions between nodal extracellular matrix proteins and Nfasc186 support node formation, and while the former is considered the dominant mechanism, the latter can partially rescue nodal Nav clustering in the absence of axo-glial junctions (Susuki et al., 2013; Amor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Susuki et al., 2013 and Amor et al., 2017.

claim: In the CNS, paranodal axo-glial junctions are considered the dominant mechanism for node formation.
source: Mechanisms of node assembly are similarly redundant in the CNS. There, both paranodal axo-glial junctions and specialised interactions between nodal extracellular matrix proteins and Nfasc186 support node formation, and while the former is considered the dominant mechanism, the latter can partially rescue nodal Nav clustering in the absence of axo-glial junctions (Susuki et al., 2013; Amor et al., 2017).
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the CNS, interactions between nodal extracellular matrix proteins and Nfasc186 can partially rescue nodal Nav clustering in the absence of axo-glial junctions.
source: Mechanisms of node assembly are similarly redundant in the CNS. There, both paranodal axo-glial junctions and specialised interactions between nodal extracellular matrix proteins and Nfasc186 support node formation, and while the former is considered the dominant mechanism, the latter can partially rescue nodal Nav clustering in the absence of axo-glial junctions (Susuki et al., 2013; Amor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Susuki et al., 2013 and Amor et al., 2017.

claim: Like heminodes, early cluster assembly depends on the interaction between Schwann cell-secreted gliomedin and neuronal Nfasc186.
source: Like heminodes, early cluster assembly depends on the interaction between Schwann cell-secreted gliomedin and neuronal Nfasc186, and also like heminodes, they are not essential for node formation since nodes are still formed in the absence of gliomedin (Feinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of Nfasc186 for early cluster formation and prior knowledge about gliomedin's role.

claim: Early clusters are not essential for node formation since nodes are still formed in the absence of gliomedin.
source: Like heminodes, early cluster assembly depends on the interaction between Schwann cell-secreted gliomedin and neuronal Nfasc186, and also like heminodes, they are not essential for node formation since nodes are still formed in the absence of gliomedin (Feinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Feinberg et al., 2010.

claim: The clustering activity of gliomedin is negatively regulated by proteolytic cleavage by BMP1/Tolloid-like proteases.
source: A recent study has demonstrated that the clustering activity of gliomedin is negatively regulated by proteolytic cleavage by BMP1/Tolloid-like proteases (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibition of BMP and Tolloid-like proteases results in enhanced formation of early clusters but does not affect myelination or node assembly.
source: Inhibition of BMP and Tolloid-like proteases results in enhanced formation of early clusters but does not affect myelination or node assembly (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Early cluster assembly was restricted to large calibre, A-type Neurofilament (NF200)-positive axons in the in vitro co-culture system.
source: Interestingly, we observed that in our in vitro co-culture system, early cluster assembly was restricted to large calibre, A-type Neurofilament (NF200)-positive axons (data not shown), which typically become myelinated in vivo (Lawson et al., 1984; Perry et al., 1991; Lawson and Waddell, 1991).
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Large calibre, A-type Neurofilament (NF200)-positive axons typically become myelinated in vivo.
source: Interestingly, we observed that in our in vitro co-culture system, early cluster assembly was restricted to large calibre, A-type Neurofilament (NF200)-positive axons (data not shown), which typically become myelinated in vivo (Lawson et al., 1984; Perry et al., 1991; Lawson and Waddell, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lawson et al., 1984; Perry et al., 1991; Lawson and Waddell, 1991.

claim: In peripheral nerves, early clusters do not assemble on unmyelinated C-type fibres in Remak bundles.
source: This is consistent with the previous observation that in peripheral nerves, early clusters do not assemble on unmyelinated C-type fibres in Remak bundles (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), and supports the view that their formation is restricted to axons that are destined to be myelinated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claim: Early cluster formation is restricted to axons that are destined to be myelinated.
source: This is consistent with the previous observation that in peripheral nerves, early clusters do not assemble on unmyelinated C-type fibres in Remak bundles (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020), and supports the view that their formation is restricted to axons that are destined to be myelinated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that early clusters form only on NF200-positive axons and not on C-type fibers.

claim: The assembly of evenly spaced early clusters of nodal proteins (also referred to as pre-nodes) has been observed in pre-myelinated CNS axons.
source: The assembly of evenly spaced early clusters of nodal proteins (also referred to as pre-nodes) has been observed in pre-myelinated CNS axons (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CNS and PNS early clusters assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes.
source: There are many similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters: (i) they assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes; (ii) they assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo; (iii) glial-derived secreted factors promote their assembly; (iv) they persist after the onset of myelination; and (v) they enhance axonal conduction velocity (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CNS and PNS early clusters assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo.
source: There are many similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters: (i) they assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes; (ii) they assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo; (iii) glial-derived secreted factors promote their assembly; (iv) they persist after the onset of myelination; and (v) they enhance axonal conduction velocity (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Glial-derived secreted factors promote the assembly of CNS and PNS early clusters.
source: There are many similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters: (i) they assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes; (ii) they assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo; (iii) glial-derived secreted factors promote their assembly; (iv) they persist after the onset of myelination; and (v) they enhance axonal conduction velocity (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CNS and PNS early clusters persist after the onset of myelination.
source: There are many similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters: (i) they assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes; (ii) they assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo; (iii) glial-derived secreted factors promote their assembly; (iv) they persist after the onset of myelination; and (v) they enhance axonal conduction velocity (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CNS and PNS early clusters enhance axonal conduction velocity.
source: There are many similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters: (i) they assemble before myelination in vitro and in vivo and share a similar molecular composition and size to mature nodes; (ii) they assemble on neurons that typically become myelinated in vivo; (iii) glial-derived secreted factors promote their assembly; (iv) they persist after the onset of myelination; and (v) they enhance axonal conduction velocity (Kaplan et al., 1997; Kaplan et al., 2001; Bonetto et al., 2019; Dubessy et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2015; Thetiot et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It is possible that CNS and PNS early clusters share a similar developmental role.
source: It is possible that CNS and PNS early clusters share a similar developmental role.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarities between CNS and PNS early clusters.

claim: A clear difference between CNS and PNS early clusters is that assembly of early clusters in the PNS requires neuronal Nfasc186, whereas in the CNS it does not.
source: Nevertheless, a clear difference is that assembly of early clusters in the PNS requires neuronal Nfasc186, whereas in the CNS it does not (Freeman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the authors' experiments showing Nfasc dependency in PNS and supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2015 for CNS.

claim: PNS early clusters are highly dynamic structures that exchange both Nfasc186 and β1-Nav with the axonal surface pool by lateral diffusion.
source: Our study has revealed that PNS early clusters are highly dynamic structures that exchange both Nfasc186 and β1-Nav with the axonal surface pool by lateral diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP and FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Nodal protein recruitment to early clusters does not occur by direct vesicular delivery.
source: Nodal protein recruitment to early clusters does not occur by direct vesicular delivery.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments showing recovery is prevented when lateral diffusion is blocked, and by nocodazole experiments showing vesicle transport disruption does not affect recovery.

claim: Nfasc186 is recruited to heminodes from an existing axonal surface pool.
source: This extends previous reports indicating that Nfasc186 is recruited to heminodes from an existing axonal surface pool.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and confirmed by the authors' FRAP/FLIP experiments.

claim: Delivery of Nav to nascent nodes reportedly occurs via vesicular transport.
source: In contrast, delivery of Nav to nascent nodes reportedly occurs via vesicular transport, but previous studies focussed on the larger, pore-forming α subunit, rather than the smaller, regulatory β subunit of Nav.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic ablation of β1-Nav does not prevent the delivery of Nav α subunits to CNS and PNS nodes of Ranvier.
source: Genetic ablation of β1-Nav does not prevent the delivery of Nav α subunits to CNS and PNS nodes of Ranvier (Chen et al., 2004), demonstrating that the two subunits can be independently delivered to nodes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2004.

claim: Nav α and β subunits can be independently delivered to nodes.
source: Genetic ablation of β1-Nav does not prevent the delivery of Nav α subunits to CNS and PNS nodes of Ranvier (Chen et al., 2004), demonstrating that the two subunits can be independently delivered to nodes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nav α subunits reach nodes even without β1-Nav.

claim: It is possible that Nav α and β subunits might follow different delivery routes to nodes.
source: It is thus possible that the two might follow different delivery routes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the subunits can be independently delivered.

claim: Full-length Nfasc186 is delivered to heminodes by lateral diffusion from the flanking unmyelinated axon.
source: We have provided the first direct demonstration that full-length Nfasc186 is not only delivered to heminodes by lateral diffusion from the flanking unmyelinated axon, but also rapidly exchanges between heminodes at the axonal pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments showing recovery is predominantly from the unmyelinated side (Figure 3D, F, G).

claim: Full-length Nfasc186 rapidly exchanges between heminodes and the axonal pool.
source: We have provided the first direct demonstration that full-length Nfasc186 is not only delivered to heminodes by lateral diffusion from the flanking unmyelinated axon, but also rapidly exchanges between heminodes at the axonal pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery at heminodes (Figure 3).

claim: The ability of both early clusters and heminodes to exchange Nfasc186 with the unmyelinated axon is consistent with their ability to merge.
source: The ability of both early clusters and heminodes to exchange Nfasc186 with the unmyelinated axon is consistent with their ability to merge.
evidence: This is inferred from the dynamic properties of both structures and the observation of fusion events.

claim: Axo-glial structural specialisations, and particularly paranodal axo-glial junctions, determine the extent of lateral mobility of Nfasc186 at nodal complexes.
source: Our study provides direct evidence that axo-glial structural specialisations, and particularly paranodal axo-glial junctions, determine the extent of lateral mobility of Nfasc186 at nodal complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments in Caspr-null mice showing increased mobility at nodes (Figure 4).

claim: In the absence of axo-glial junctions, mature nodes revert to a more immature state, reacquiring the ability to exchange Nfasc186 with the axonal surface pool by lateral diffusion.
source: In the absence of axo-glial junctions, mature nodes revert to a more immature state, reacquiring the ability to exchange Nfasc186 with the axonal surface pool by lateral diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing increased recovery at Caspr-null nodes (Figure 4).

claim: The strength and nature of the molecular interactions between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins at mature nodes and early clusters are not intrinsically different, but are modulated by the presence of the axo-glial complex.
source: This has two important implications: first, it indicates that the strength and nature of the molecular interactions taking place between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins (e.g., cytoskeletal scaffold proteins) at mature nodes and early clusters are not intrinsically different, but that they are modulated by the presence of the axo-glial complex; second, it reveals that in the absence of axo-glial junctions, Nfasc186 could diffuse through the internodal regions of myelinated axons, and could, conceivably, exchange between adjacent nodes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nodes without junctions behave more like early clusters.

claim: In the absence of axo-glial junctions, Nfasc186 could diffuse through the internodal regions of myelinated axons.
source: This has two important implications: first, it indicates that the strength and nature of the molecular interactions taking place between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins (e.g., cytoskeletal scaffold proteins) at mature nodes and early clusters are not intrinsically different, but that they are modulated by the presence of the axo-glial complex; second, it reveals that in the absence of axo-glial junctions, Nfasc186 could diffuse through the internodal regions of myelinated axons, and could, conceivably, exchange between adjacent nodes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Nfasc186 can laterally diffuse in the absence of junctions.

claim: In the absence of axo-glial junctions, Nfasc186 could conceivably exchange between adjacent nodes.
source: This has two important implications: first, it indicates that the strength and nature of the molecular interactions taking place between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins (e.g., cytoskeletal scaffold proteins) at mature nodes and early clusters are not intrinsically different, but that they are modulated by the presence of the axo-glial complex; second, it reveals that in the absence of axo-glial junctions, Nfasc186 could diffuse through the internodal regions of myelinated axons, and could, conceivably, exchange between adjacent nodes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Nfasc186 can laterally diffuse in the absence of junctions.

claim: Despite being closely contacted by periaxin-positive, myelinating Schwann cells, and despite their focal accumulation of gliomedin, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli.
source: An important structural difference between early clusters and more mature nodal complexes that has been revealed by this study is that, despite being closely contacted by periaxin-positive, myelinating Schwann cells, and despite their focal accumulation of gliomedin, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli, which are known to emerge at early stages of Schwann cell maturation before the start of myelin ensheathment (Gatto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining showing absence of microvillar markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and CLEM (Figure 2C).

claim: Schwann cell microvilli emerge at early stages of Schwann cell maturation before the start of myelin ensheathment.
source: An important structural difference between early clusters and more mature nodal complexes that has been revealed by this study is that, despite being closely contacted by periaxin-positive, myelinating Schwann cells, and despite their focal accumulation of gliomedin, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli, which are known to emerge at early stages of Schwann cell maturation before the start of myelin ensheathment (Gatto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gatto et al., 2003.

claim: The absence of Schwann cell microvilli likely contributes to the highly dynamic properties of early clusters, including their ability to migrate towards and readily merge with heminodes.
source: The absence of Schwann cell microvilli likely contributes to the highly dynamic properties of early clusters, including their ability to migrate towards and readily merge with heminodes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between early clusters and heminodes/nodes.

claim: This is the first documented example of long-range movement of membrane-bound protein complexes along the axon, excluding heminodes.
source: To our knowledge, and excluding heminodes, this is the first documented example of long-range movement of membrane-bound protein complexes along the axon.
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their knowledge of the literature.

claim: Schwann cells contacting early clusters appear to migrate along the axon at similar rates to early clusters.
source: Although we cannot exclude an axon-based mechanism, based on our observation that Schwann cells contacting early clusters also appear to migrate along the axon at similar rates (data not shown), we hypothesise that these cells might be responsible for early cluster motility.
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Schwann cells might be responsible for early cluster motility.
source: Although we cannot exclude an axon-based mechanism, based on our observation that Schwann cells contacting early clusters also appear to migrate along the axon at similar rates (data not shown), we hypothesise that these cells might be responsible for early cluster motility.

claim: Early clusters of nodal protein complexes represent the earliest Nav clustering event in the PNS.
source: In conclusion, we describe a new aspect of the diverse redundant mechanisms that appears to be a characteristic of a critical stage in the development of the vertebrate nervous system, namely the assembly of nodes of Ranvier. We have presented evidence that early clusters of nodal protein complexes represent the earliest Nav clustering event in the PNS, that their assembly is at an early developmental stage of myelination, and that they can actively contribute to the assembly of nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by temporal analysis showing early clusters appear before heminodes and nodes.
